text: RMGAP: Benchmarking the Generalization of Reward Models across Diverse Preferences Yangyang Zhou1,† Yi-Chen Li2,3 1 Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications 2 National Key Laboratory for Novel Software Technology, Nanjing University, China 3 School of Artificial Intelligence, Nanjing University, China † Correspondence: zhouyangyang@bupt.edu.cn Abstract Reinforcement Learning from Human Feed- back has become the standard paradigm for language model alignment, where reward mod- els directly determine alignment effectiveness. In this work, we focus on how to evaluate the generalizability of reward models. By "gen- eralizability", we mean the ability of RMs to correctly rank responses to align with di- verse user preferences. However, existing re- ward model benchmarks are typically designed around a universal preference, failing to as- sess this generalization. To address this crit- ical gap, we introduce RMGAP, a benchmark comprising 1,097 instances across Chat, Writ- ing, Reasoning, and Safety domains. Since different users exhibit diverse preferences for the same task, we first generate four distinct responses with different linguistic profiles for each collected prompt. However, the original prompt set lacks the specificity to convey differ- ent preferences. We therefore construct tailored prompts by contrasting these candidates and designing scenarios in which one response be- comes the uniquely appropriate choice. More- over, we observe that users often express the same preference using different phrasings, and thus extend each prompt with two paraphrased variants. Our evaluation of 24 state-of-the-art RMs reveals their substantial limitations: even the best RM achieves only 49.27% Best-of-N accuracy, highlighting considerable room for improvement in reward model generalization. Related data and code are available at https: //github.com/nanzhi84/RMGAP. 1 Introduction As Large Language Models (LLMs) become inte- grated into diverse applications (OpenAI, 2025; Bai et al., 2022b), alignment is no longer about match- ing a single universal notion of "helpful" or "harm- less" (Poddar et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024c; Wang et al., 2024). Therefore, the quality of the reward model directly determines the effectiveness of the alignment, yet it remains unclear whether RMs can generalize across diverse user preferences. Current reward model benchmarks predomi- nantly rely on the assumption of a universal prefer- ence (Lambert et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024b; Zhou et al., 2024). As illustrated in Figure 1 (left), these benchmarks present a generic prompt and score responses based on their overall quality. Although recent work has extended evaluation to subjective writing quality (Ying et al., 2025), it still relies on a fixed evaluation criterion. However, these benchmarks overlook a critical fact: different users have different preferences, and the standard for what constitutes a good response varies accord- ingly. This makes these benchmarks fail to assess whether reward models truly capture diverse user preferences and can flexibly adjust their criteria for different needs. Consequently, the generalization of reward models remains largely unexplored. We argue that a comprehensive benchmark should explicitly evaluate preference generalization along two axes: (i) Sensitivity to diverse prefer- ences: A reward model should possess sufficient sensitivity to recognize distinct demands within user queries to award higher rewards to responses that align with those specific preferences. To address this gap, we introduce RM- GAP (Reward Model Generalization Across Preferences), the first benchmark specifically de- signed to systematically evaluate reward model generalization across diverse preferences. As il- lustrated in Figure 1 (right), RMGAP constructs specific prompts that elicit distinct preferences, enabling direct assessment of whether RMs can adapt their judgments to different user preferences. RMGAP comprises 1,097 instances spanning four domains: Chat, Writing, Reasoning, and Safety, amounting to a total of 4,388 responses and 13,164 prompts. The construction pipeline consists of four steps: (1) We first select and filter seed prompts from open-source datasets. (2) For each selected prompt, we deterministically assign four well- separated style profiles and generate four distinct responses using a pool of seven frontier LLMs. (3) To ensure alignment between instruction and re- sponse, we synthesize a specific prompt tailored to each response’s intended preference. (4) Finally, we extend each prompt with two paraphrased vari- ants to better reflect the diversity of human expres- sions observed in practice. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 24 frontier reward models on RMGAP, assessing them with three metrics: (1) Pair accuracy, which mea- sures the accuracy of pairwise preference compar- isons; (2) Best of N (BoN) accuracy, which evalu- ates the model’s ability to select the best response from multiple candidates; and (3) Ranking consis- tency, which quantifies whether models maintain stable rankings across paraphrased prompt vari- ants. On this dataset, we observe that scalar reward models tend to better balance accuracy and consis- tency, whereas generative RMs appear to exhibit a clearer trade-off between these two metrics under paraphrase. We further observe that Writing is the most challenging domain for generative RMs on RMGAP, while Reasoning appears to be the most difficult domain for both scalar and DPO models. Additionally, our results suggest that high pairwise accuracy does not necessarily translate into effec- tive Best-of-N selection. Our work makes the following key contributions: • We introduce RMGAP, the first benchmark specifically designed to evaluate reward model generalization across diverse preferences, com- prising 1,097 instances spanning Chat, Writing, Reasoning, and Safety. • We develop a scalable multi-stage construction pipeline that generates prompts with diverse pref- erence requirements and responses with distinct profiles across five linguistic dimensions. • We evaluate 24 representative reward models us- ing pairwise accuracy, Best-of-N accuracy, and ranking consistency, revealing substantial room for improvement as even the best model achieves only 69.97% pairwise accuracy and 49.27% Best- of-N accuracy. 2 2 Related Work Reward Modeling Paradigms Reward models provide reward signals for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. Prevail- ing reward modeling paradigms can be broadly cat- egorized into three types: (a) Scalar RMs are typ- ically constructed by adding a classification head to a large pre-trained language model. These mod- els are then trained on curated preference datasets to produce a scalar reward, often based on the Bradley-Terry model (Bradley and Terry, 1952; Ouyang et al., 2022). (b) Implicit RMs bypass explicit reward modeling, directly optimizing the policy on preference data for greater stability and simplicity (Rafailov et al., 2023). (c) Generative RMs construct the reward signal by leveraging the generation capabilities of the LLM itself, which can be further divided into two categories: LLM as judge (Mahan et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025a), which prompts the model to di- rectly output a judgment, and token probability based methods (Zhang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025b), which use the model’s log probability of generating specific tokens as the reward.

Reward Model Evaluation Evaluating reward models is critical for advancing LLM alignment. RewardBench (Lambert et al., 2025) established a foundational framework across chat, reasoning, and safety domains. RM-BENCH (Liu et al., 2024b) emphasized assessing RMs’ sensitivity to subtle content changes and robustness against style bi- ases. RMB (Zhou et al., 2024) expanded evalua- tion to 49 real-world scenarios and proposed the Best-of-N paradigm to better reflect alignment op- timization. WritingPreferenceBench (Ying et al., 2025) explored subjective aesthetic judgments in cross-cultural creative writing. However, existing benchmarks predominantly evaluate RMs on a sin- gle, universal preference and do not systematically assess generalization capabilities. In contrast, RM- GAP is the first to comprehensively evaluate reward model generalization across diverse preferences and varied linguistic expressions. 3 Data Construction of RMGAP 3.1 Overview Our benchmark is designed to systematically evalu- ate reward model generalization across four do- mains (Chat, Writing, Reasoning, Safety). We obtain 3,371 candidate seed prompts via filter- ing from established domain-specific datasets and subsequently construct 1,097 evaluation instances. Each instance comprises four stylistically distinct responses, each paired with a group of three seman- tically equivalent prompts that elicit the specific preference of that response. Table 5 in Appendix E summarizes the dataset statistics across domains. As illustrated in Figure 2, we build each instance via a multi-stage pipeline with quality control pro- cedures to ensure data quality, diversity, and relia- bility. 3.2 Prompt Selection Source Datasets We source seed prompts from established benchmarks to ensure domain diver- sity and task authenticity. For Chat, we draw from Arena-Hard (Li et al., 2024a,b), which pro- vides challenging user queries from real-world in- teractions. The Writing domain uses creative writ- ing prompts from WritingBench (Wu et al., 2025) and prompts from Writing-Preference-Bench (Ying et al., 2025). For Reasoning, we source mathemat- ical problems from MATH-500 (Lightman et al., 2023) and coding tasks from HumanEval (Chen, 2021). For the Safety domain, we use prompts from XSTest (Röttger et al., 2024) and FalseReject (Zhang et al., 2025). Filtering Procedure We filter prompts following prior work on preference data construction (Lee et al., 2024). We first apply regular expressions to discard prompts containing explicit persona instruc- tions (to avoid confounding preference signals) or non-English content. We then perform both exact and semantic deduplication, keeping only one rep- resentative in each group of prompts with identical surface forms or with high cosine similarity in the embedding space. After filtering, we retain 3,371 prompts, which serve as candidate seed prompts for constructing evaluation instances. This yields one evaluation instance consist- ing of 4 responses and 12 prompts. 3.3.2 Response Generation We generate stylistic responses by assigning each seed prompt four distinct style profiles from a struc- tured stylistic space. Drawing on register variation theory (Biber, 1995), we define five linguistic di- mensions, each discretized into five levels: • Formality: casual, informal, neutral, formal, highly formal. • Conciseness: terse, concise, moderate, detailed, verbose. • Technicality: layman, accessible, semi-technical, technical, highly specialized. • Objectivity: highly subjective, subjective, bal- anced, objective, strictly objective. • Structural Coherence: fragmented, loose, orga- nized, well-structured, rigorous. For each seed prompt, we deterministically gen- erate four distinct combinations of levels, while enforcing a minimum Manhattan distance of 8 be- tween any two profiles. We incorporate these speci- fications into generation templates and generate re- sponses with a pool of seven frontier LLMs, which increases response diversity and reduces depen- dence on a single generator. As shown in Table 5, generated responses exhibit clear length variation correlated with stylistic dimensions, particularly Conciseness and Structural Coherence. 3.3.3 Prompt Construction To evaluate whether reward models can generalize to prompts with explicit preference instructions, we construct a tailored prompt for each stylistically controlled response. Specifically, we input all four responses of an instance simultaneously into a gen- erator sampled from our model pool. We instruct the model to distinguish the stylistic differences among the responses and synthesize a dedicated user query for each response that explicitly targets the preference exhibited in that response. F Reward Model Evaluation Details This section provides implementation details for the reward model evaluation methods used in our experiments. F.1 EndoRM EndoRM (Endogenous Reward Model) leverages the inherent language modeling capability of LLMs as an implicit reward signal (Li et al., 2025b). Given a prompt x and response y = (t1, t2, . . . , tn), the reward score is computed as: Score(x, y) = Aggregate ({log P(ti|x, t<i)}n i=1) We use discounted sum aggregation: Score = Pn i=1 γi−1 · log P(ti|x, t<i), with discount factor γ = 0.93. F.2 Generative Verifier RM Generative Verifier RM frames reward modeling as a binary classification task (Zhang et al., 2024). The model evaluates whether a response is “good” based on relevance and factuality criteria, answer- ing with “YES” or “NO”. The reward score is the mean log-probability of generating “YES”: Score(x, y) = 1 |YES| X t∈YES log P(t|prompt) F.3 GenRM-Pointwise GenRM-Pointwise solicits an explicit quality judg- ment by prompting the model to output an integer score between 1 and 10. The score is extracted via regex pattern matching and clamped to the valid range. If extraction fails after 3 attempts, a default score of 5 is assigned. F.4 GenRM-Listwise GenRM-Listwise performs comparative evaluation by presenting four responses simultaneously and asking the model to rank them from best to worst. To mitigate positional bias, responses are randomly shuffled before presentation, and final scores are mapped back to the original order.
